records.statement: Goertzel and Pitt's paper of February 2012 states that the authors believe, on qualitative grounds, that an open approach to developing artificial general intelligence is probably preferable to a closed one, citing the wider critique an open codebase receives.
records.qualification: The paper concerns open-source AGI code and development, before model weights were the object of the debate; the authors say they do not argue the point rigorously and name the risk of malevolent groups forking an open project. A statement of the authors' intuition, not evidence that open development is safer.

evidence.locator: Section 2, "Is open or closed AGI development safer?"
evidence.passage: We do believe intuitively that the open approach is probably preferable, but our reasons are qualitative and we recognize there are also qualitative arguments in the opposite direction.
The authors cite Linus's law ("Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow") and write that a closed approach makes it very hard to obtain the level of critique a public, open codebase receives.
we also understand the risk of terrorist groups or other malevolent agents forking an open source AGI project and creating something terribly dangerous and destructive

records.statement: Alexander's post of 17 December 2015 argues, in response to the founding of OpenAI, that making AI findings open source lets the least careful developer set the pace and, if takeoff is fast and control difficult, makes catastrophe more likely, and that the benefit of spreading power does not justify that risk.

engagement.rationale: Answers the premise that wide distribution of AI prevents concentration of power, arguing it lets the least cautious developer decide.

records.qualification: The argument is conditional on hard takeoff and difficult control; the post names OpenAI's founding statement and a press interview with its co-chairs, which are not evidence here. It concerns open-sourcing findings and designs, before open model weights.

evidence.passage: The risk is letting the most careless person in the world determine the speed of AI research
The risk is that in a world with hard takeoffs and difficult control problems, you get superhuman AIs that hurl everybody off cliffs.
But the benefits just aren’t clear enough to justify that level of risk.

records.statement: Bostrom's paper of 2017 argues that, while short-term effects of openness appear mostly beneficial, openness about source code, science and possibly capability could make the race to advanced AI more closely competitive and so make it harder to pause for, or to afford, safety measures.

engagement.rationale: Answers the premise that wider access and scrutiny improve safety by arguing that openness tightens competition and so squeezes safety work.

records.qualification: The paper distinguishes forms of openness and judges openness about safety measures and goals plausibly positive; it calls itself a preliminary analysis. It is about openness in AI development generally, not model weights specifically.

evidence.passage: Others (openness about source code, science, and possibly capability) could lead to a tightening of the competitive situation around the time of the introduction of advanced AI

evidence.locator: Section "Openness making AI development race more closely competitive", PDF p. 8
evidence.passage: It would make it harder to pause towards the end in order to implement or test a safety mechanism. It would also make it harder to use any safety mechanism that reduces efﬁciency.
Short-term impacts of increased openness appear mostly socially beneﬁcial in expectation.
evidence.note: The paper's own qualification of its finding.

records.statement: Bostrom's paper of 2017 argues that in a closely competitive race a larger pool of developers is likely to contain one willing to proceed without adequate safeguards, and that competition makes it harder for any developer to accept safety measures that cost performance.

engagement.rationale: Argues that competitive pressure, not market reward, governs how much safety a developer can afford.

records.qualification: The passage is a model-level argument about race dynamics under openness, not an empirical finding about developer behaviour.

evidence.locator: Section "Openness making AI development race more closely competitive", PDF p. 6
evidence.passage: The larger the pool of competitors, the harder it would be for them to all coordinate to avoid a risk race to the bottom.

records.statement: Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman's technical report of 2013 presents a model in which teams racing to build a powerful AI are incentivised to skimp on safety precautions, and in which more teams and more enmity between them increase the danger of an AI disaster.

time.note: Title page of the FHI technical report; journal version (2016) not read.

engagement.rationale: Models developer incentives directly and finds that the incentive to win pushes precautions down.

records.qualification: A stylised game-theoretic model with assumptions the authors state (a powerful AI built by the winning team, a disaster probability rising as precautions fall); it does not measure any developer's incentives.

evidence.passage: each team is incentivised to finish first – by skimping on safety precautions if need be.
Having extra development teams and extra enmity between teams can increase the danger of an AI-disaster

records.statement: Askell, Brundage and Hadfield's paper of July 2019 argues that AI companies have the market, liability and regulatory incentives to develop responsibly that companies in other industries have, but that these appear weaker for AI, and that competition can lead companies to underinvest in safety, making responsible development a collective action problem.

engagement.rationale: States the market-incentive premise (consumers, reputation, liability) and argues competition and information gaps weaken it.

records.qualification: The paper accepts that market incentives for safety exist and argues they are insufficient under competition; it does not address catastrophic risk specifically and proposes cooperation strategies rather than measuring incentives.

evidence.passage: We argue that AI companies have the same incentives to develop AI systems responsibly, although they appear to be weaker than they are in other industries.
competitive pressures could incentivize AI companies to underinvest in ensuring their systems are safe, secure, and have a positive social impact.
Market forces alone may not always incentivize companies to invest the appropriate amount into ensuring their products are safe.

records.statement: Leahy's EleutherAI post of 2 June 2021 argues that releasing a GPT-3-like model openly is a net good because it enables safety research on large models, and that keeping such technology from well-funded bad actors is futile once its feasibility is published.
records.qualification: The post limits its case to models of roughly GPT-3 scale and says EleutherAI would not release a far larger model whose capabilities no one could know; it presents itself as a summary, not a full treatment.

evidence.passage: the construction and release of such a model is a net good for society, because it will enable more safety-relevant research to be done on such models.
attempting to keep this technology out of the hands of bad actors is futile

records.statement: Narayanan and Kapoor's post of 6 March 2023, written after the leak of Meta's LLaMA weights, argues that the cost of producing disinformation is not the bottleneck for influence operations, so that the risk of malicious misuse of open language models is lower than widely assumed, which they call an argument in favour of open-sourcing.
records.qualification: Limited to disinformation and spam; the authors say they take no position on whether models should be open-sourced, misuse being only one factor.

evidence.passage: The bottleneck isn't the cost of producing disinfo, which is already very low.
If we are correct about the risk of malicious misuse being lower than widely assumed, that’s an argument in favor of open-sourcing LLMs.
we don’t have an opinion on whether they should be open-sourced

records.statement: The Llama 2 paper of 18 July 2023 by Touvron and other Meta authors states that the authors believe the open release of large language models, when done safely, will be a net benefit to society, and that an open approach and collaboration will make the models better and safer.
records.qualification: A developer's statement about its own release, made in the release paper; the authors also state that the model carries risks and that testing could not cover all scenarios. Not evidence of the release's effects.

evidence.passage: We believe that the open release of LLMs, when done safely, will be a net benefit to society.

evidence.locator: Section 5.3, Responsible Release Strategy, PDF p. 35
evidence.passage: Collaboration will make these models better and safer.

records.statement: The statement of support published by Meta on 18 July 2023 states that responsible and open innovation brings visibility, scrutiny and trust to AI technologies and that opening the Llama models will let everyone benefit.
records.qualification: A signed statement: the record is what the statement says, not each signatory's view. It speaks of scrutiny and trust rather than of catastrophic risk.

evidence.passage: Responsible and open innovation gives us all a stake in the AI development process, bringing visibility, scrutiny and trust to these technologies.

records.statement: The Joint Statement on AI Safety and Openness hosted by Mozilla and dated 31 October 2023 states that increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, and that openness is an antidote, not a poison, for AI safety and security.
records.qualification: A signed statement: the record is what the statement says, not each signatory's view; the statement itself says its signatories hold different views on how open-source AI should be managed. It also states that open models can be abused.

evidence.passage: increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
When it comes to AI safety and security, openness is an antidote, not a poison.

records.statement: Seger and co-authors' paper of September 2023 argues that, although open-sourcing has historically brought net benefits, for some highly capable foundation models likely to be developed soon it may pose risks extreme enough to outweigh the benefits, partly because release is irreversible and safeguards can be removed.

engagement.rationale: States the benefits attributed to openness and argues that removable safeguards and irreversibility outweigh them for highly capable models.

records.qualification: The argument is limited to some future highly capable models; the paper recommends alternatives that preserve open-source benefits, and states that authorship does not entail endorsement of every claim.

evidence.passage: we argue that for some highly capable foundation models likely to be developed in the near future, open-sourcing may pose sufficiently extreme risks to outweigh the benefits.
open-source AI model release is irreversible; there is no “undo” function if significant harms materialize.

records.statement: Gopal and co-authors' paper of 25 October 2023 reports a hackathon in which a version of Llama-2-70B tuned to remove safeguards gave some participants nearly all key information needed to obtain the 1918 influenza virus, and states that releasing the weights of advanced foundation models will trigger the proliferation of knowledge sufficient to acquire pandemic agents.

engagement.rationale: Answers the premise that safeguards and existing availability keep marginal misuse risk low, with an exercise on a model whose safeguards were removed.

records.qualification: Read in its abstract only; the paper's method and its comparison with information already available elsewhere were not checked. A statement of the authors' conclusion, not evidence that it is correct.

evidence.passage: Our results suggest that releasing the weights of advanced foundation models, no matter how robustly safeguarded, will trigger the proliferation of knowledge sufficient to acquire pandemic agents and other biological weapons.

records.statement: Kapoor, Bommasani and co-authors' position paper of 27 February 2024 states that open foundation models bring significant benefits, including a wider distribution of decision-making power, and proposes a framework for assessing their marginal risk relative to closed models and pre-existing technologies, which it says explains why that marginal risk is low in some cases.
records.qualification: The paper also finds that current research is insufficient to characterise the marginal risk for most misuse vectors and that the risk will change as capabilities and defences change; it does not state that open release adds little risk in general. Most developed is an editorial judgement among the located texts.

evidence.passage: Open foundation models present significant benefits, with some caveats, that span innovation, competition, the distribution of decision-making power, and transparency.
The framework helps explain why the marginal risk is low in some cases
we find that current research is insufficient to effectively characterize the marginal risk of open foundation models relative to pre-existing technologies.

records.statement: Eiras and co-authors' paper of 14 May 2024 argues that, overall, the benefits of open-source generative AI outweigh its risks, and that open source reduces the likelihood of existential risk by contributing to technical alignment and maintaining the balance of power.
records.qualification: The existential-risk argument is stated for a long-term stage and partly conditioned on technical alignment being achieved; the paper also lists net-negative features of open models, such as that they cannot be rolled back.

evidence.passage: We argue that, overall, the benefits of open-source Gen AI outweigh its risks.
open source (i) reduces the likelihood of existential risk by contributing to the development of technical alignment and maintaining the balance of power

records.statement: Zuckerberg's essay of 23 July 2024 states that open source AI will be safer than the alternatives, because open systems can be widely scrutinised, and that a world in which AI is widely deployed lets larger actors check the power of smaller bad actors.
records.qualification: The essay is also an account of Meta's commercial reasons for releasing Llama; it is the statement of the developer releasing the models, not evidence of their effects. The page carries an update date of 27 January 2025 and the wording read is the current one.

evidence.locator: Section "Why Open Source AI Is Good for the World"
evidence.passage: There is an ongoing debate about the safety of open source AI models, and my view is that open source AI will be safer than the alternatives.
I think it will be better to live in a world where AI is widely deployed so that larger actors can check the power of smaller bad actors.

records.statement: Narayanan and Kapoor's post of 12 March 2024 argues that defences against misuse must be located mainly outside models, so that there might not be a big difference between the safety implications of open and closed release strategies.
records.qualification: Concerned with misuse, not loss of control; the authors call for a more rigorous assessment of marginal risk rather than concluding that it is low.

evidence.passage: If safety is not primarily a model property and defenses must reside elsewhere, then there might not be a big difference between the safety implications of open and closed release strategies.

records.statement: Howard's essay of 10 July 2023 argues that stringent licensing of AI models would concentrate power, and that supporting open-source model development could increase overall safety by letting more people with varied expertise identify and counter threats.
records.qualification: The essay answers the white paper "Frontier AI Regulation" and argues for regulating applications rather than development; the safety claim is stated as a possibility ("could").

evidence.passage: Broad participation could allow more people with a wider variety of expertise to help identify and counter threats, thus increasing overall safety
Proposals for stringent AI model licensing and surveillance will likely be ineffective or counterproductive, concentrating power in unsustainable ways

records.statement: Andreessen's essay of June 2023 argues that open source AI should be allowed to proliferate without regulatory barriers, that restricting AI is infeasible because the knowledge is already widely available, and that misuse should be met by law and by using AI defensively.
records.missing: A statement that open release reduces overall risk or adds little marginal risk; the essay argues that restriction is infeasible and that misuse should be met by law and defensive AI.
records.qualification: Recorded as bearing on the proposition: the essay argues against restricting open source and for defensive use, but does not state that open release reduces risk or adds little marginal risk.

evidence.passage: Open source AI should be allowed to freely proliferate and compete with both big AI companies and startups. There should be no regulatory barriers to open source whatsoever.
there’s another way to prevent such actions, and that’s by using AI as a defensive tool.

records.statement: The NTIA report of July 2024 assesses the marginal risks and benefits of widely available model weights relative to closed models and other technologies, concludes that current evidence is not sufficient to determine that restrictions are warranted or that they will never be appropriate, and recommends that the government monitor risks and keep the capacity to act.
records.missing: A conclusion that open weights reduce risk or add little marginal risk; the report leaves the question open and recommends monitoring.
records.qualification: A government report produced under Executive Order 14110; it adopts the marginal-risk framing but reaches no conclusion that open weights reduce risk or add little.

evidence.passage: current evidence is not sufficient to definitively determine either that restrictions on such openweight models are warranted, or that restrictions will never be appropriate in the future.

records.statement: Ng's letter in The Batch of 10 July 2024 argues that California's SB 1047 regulates AI technology instead of applications, would fail to make AI meaningfully safer and is pernicious to open source.
records.missing: A statement that open release reduces risk or adds little marginal risk.
records.qualification: Recorded as bearing on the proposition: the letter defends open source against a bill but does not state that open release reduces risk.

evidence.passage: this proposed law makes a fundamental mistake of regulating AI technology instead of AI applications, and thus would fail to make AI meaningfully safer.

records.statement: Solaiman and co-authors' OpenAI report of August 2019 states that OpenAI released GPT-2 in stages, withholding the larger models at first because of concerns about misuse such as fake news, impersonation and automated abusive content.
records.missing: An argument that open release increases overall risk; the report describes a staged release made on misuse concerns.
records.qualification: A developer's report on its own release decision; the misuse it names is below catastrophic scale.

evidence.passage: withholding larger models due to concerns about the potential for misuse, such as generating fake news content, impersonating others in email, or automating abusive social media content production

records.statement: Brundage and co-authors' report of February 2018 states that openly sharing all new AI capabilities and algorithms by default increases the power of the tools available to malicious actors, and calls for reimagining norms of openness, including pre-publication risk assessment.

engagement.rationale: States a misuse cost of default openness without answering the arguments that openness improves scrutiny or defence.

records.qualification: Concerned with research publication norms and misuse generally, before open model weights were the object; the report also records the benefits of openness and asks a question rather than prescribing closure.

evidence.passage: a downside to openly sharing all new capabilities and algorithms by default: it increases the power of tools available to malicious actors.

records.statement: Shevlane's paper of January 2022 proposes structured capability access, in which developers offer controlled interactions with AI systems instead of disseminating them openly, with the aim of preventing dangerous capabilities from being widely accessible.

engagement.rationale: Proposes restricted access as safer without engaging the scrutiny or distribution-of-power premises.

records.qualification: Argues for an alternative to open dissemination rather than against arguments for openness; the paper discusses the objection that it centralises power in developers.

evidence.passage: Instead of openly disseminating AI systems, developers facilitate controlled, arm’s length interactions with their AI systems. The aim is to prevent dangerous AI capabilities from being widely accessible

records.statement: Hendrycks, Mazeika and Woodside's overview of 21 June 2023 argues that open-sourcing an AI system with biological research capabilities could increase the risk of malicious use, and recommends that developers avoid open-sourcing the most powerful systems in favour of structured access.

engagement.rationale: Answers the premise that open release adds little marginal misuse risk by pointing to dual-use biological capabilities, where one release decides the outcome.

records.qualification: Part of a survey of catastrophic risks; the open-source passages are brief and illustrative.

evidence.passage: this could also increase the risk of malicious use if the AI system could be repurposed to develop bioweapons.

evidence.locator: Section 4, Organizational Risks, suggestions, PDF p. 33
evidence.passage: AI developers should avoid open-sourcing the most powerful systems and instead implement structured access

records.statement: Hendrycks, Mazeika and Woodside's overview of 21 June 2023 argues that competitive pressure fuels a corporate AI race in which companies race to offer the first products to market rather than the safest, and recommends safety regulation so that developers do not cut corners.

engagement.rationale: Argues that market competition rewards speed over safety, against the premise that markets reward safe products.

records.qualification: An argument from analogy and recent examples, not a measurement of incentives.

evidence.locator: Section 3.2.1, Economic Competition Undercuts Safety, PDF p. 19
evidence.passage: To obtain a competitive advantage, companies often race to offer the first products to a market rather than the safest.
Regulation holds AI developers to a common standard so that they do not cut corners on safety.

records.statement: Hendrycks's paper of 28 March 2023 argues that competitive pressures among corporations and militaries will favour AI agents with undesirable traits, and that while there are some economic incentives to make models safer, these are outweighed by the desire for performance.

engagement.rationale: States that economic incentives for safety exist and argues that competition for performance outweighs them.

records.qualification: An evolutionary argument about selection pressures; the passage on economic incentives is a judgement about current practice, not a measurement.

evidence.locator: Section "Competition could continue to erode safety", PDF p. 14
evidence.passage: While there are some economic incentives to make models safer, these are being outweighed by the desire for performance, and performance has been at the expense of many key safety properties.
Competitive pressures among corporations and militaries will give rise to AI agents that automate human roles, deceive others, and gain power.

records.statement: Bengio's post of 9 July 2024 states that open-sourcing may currently be more beneficial than detrimental to safety, but argues that as capabilities advance the decision should not rest with companies, and that the argument that good AIs would outnumber and defeat bad AIs has many flaws, including the advantage of attackers using bioweapons.

engagement.rationale: Answers the defensive-balance premise (more good AIs than bad) with the offence-defence asymmetry.

records.qualification: The post states that open-sourcing may currently be more beneficial than detrimental to safety and argues otherwise for future systems at or beyond human level.

evidence.locator: Section "For those who think that open source AGI code and weights are the solution"
evidence.passage: some have made the argument that if everyone had their own AGI, the "good AIs" would win over the "bad AIs" because there are more good people. There are many flaws in this argument.
Open-sourcing of AI systems may plausibly currently be more beneficial than detrimental to safety because they enable AI safety research in academia
evidence.note: The present-day concession that the post then limits.

records.statement: Bengio's post of 9 July 2024 answers the argument that corporations would prefer to build safe AI by stating that the problem arises when safety and profit maximisation are not aligned, citing fossil-fuel and drug companies, and that global risks are an externality for developers.

engagement.rationale: States the incentive argument as a question and answers it with the externality of global risks.

records.qualification: The historical analogies are the author's; the post does not analyse AI developers' incentives empirically.

evidence.locator: Section on the argument that engineers will only design well-behaving AIs
evidence.passage: Shouldn't corporations prefer safe AI? The problem comes when safety and profit maximization or company culture ("move fast and break things") are not aligned.

records.statement: Widder, Whittaker and West's article of 27 November 2024 argues that openness alone does not perturb the concentration of power in AI and that rhetoric around open AI is often used in ways that increase that concentration.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that open release widely distributes power.

records.qualification: Disputes the distribution-of-power premise only; the article does not assess catastrophic or misuse risk, and states that maximally open AI allows some forms of oversight and experimentation.

evidence.passage: we find that openness alone does not perturb the concentration of power in AI.
rhetoric around ‘open’ AI is frequently wielded in ways that exacerbate rather than reduce concentration of power in the AI sector.

records.statement: Hinton's Nobel banquet speech of 10 December 2024 states that there is now evidence that, if digital beings more intelligent than humans are created by companies motivated by short-term profits, safety will not be the top priority.

engagement.rationale: States the contrary of the proposition without engaging the market or liability mechanism.

records.qualification: The speech does not say what the evidence is.

evidence.passage: But we now have evidence that if they are created by companies motivated by short-term profits, our safety will not be the top priority.

records.statement: Hanson's essay of 14 April 2023 argues that the organisations that supply AIs monitor and test them in great detail because that is cheap and they are liable for damages and embarrassments, and that law and competition push them to make their AIs behave in civil, lawful ways.
records.qualification: Earliest located among this pack's records only: the dataset's economics collection (E04) records Hanson's blog posts of 2008 on the same concept, which are linked, not re-recorded. The essay also states that competition sometimes leads firms to cheat customers in ways they cannot see.

evidence.passage: These institutions usually monitor and test AIs in great detail, because that’s cheap and they are liable for damages and embarrassments caused by the AIs they produce.
Many organizations supply many AIs and they are pushed by law and competition to get their AIs to behave in civil, lawful ways that give customers more of what they want compared to alternatives.

records.statement: Narayanan and Kapoor's essay of April 2025 argues that how well developers and deployers mitigate AI accidents depends on their incentives, that in many cases market forces will provide an adequate incentive with safety regulation filling the gaps, and that poorly controlled AI will be too error-prone to make business sense.

time.note: Day not confirmed from the retrieved text.

records.qualification: The essay pairs market incentives with ordinary safety regulation and describes past safety races caused by market failure; it argues against measures specific to catastrophic risk elsewhere, not in these passages.

evidence.passage: In many cases, market forces will provide an adequate incentive, but safety regulation should fill any gaps.
Poorly controlled AI will be too error prone to make business sense.
Market success has been strongly correlated with safety.

replies.statement: Alexander's post of 17 December 2015 replies to the announcement of OpenAI, which it names and quotes.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the text addresses the other. The post also quotes a press interview with OpenAI's co-chairs, which is not evidence here.

evidence.passage: Some of the top names in Silicon Valley have just announced a new organization, OpenAI, dedicated to “advancing digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole…as broadly and evenly distributed as possible.”

replies.statement: Kapoor, Bommasani and co-authors' paper of February 2024 cites Gopal and co-authors' paper as finding that open language models can generate accurate information about pandemic pathogens, and states that such information is publicly available without open language models.
replies.qualification: A citation is not agreement; it records that the text addresses the other. The paper cites Gopal et al. and Guha et al. together as an example of researchers reaching different conclusions without a marginal-risk framework, and cites Seger et al. (2023) in the same passage as one of the works arguing that open weights enable misuse.

evidence.passage: open language models can generate accurate information about pandemic-causing pathogens (Gopal et al., 2023), yet such information is publicly available on the Internet, even without the use of open language models (Guha et al., 2023).

replies.statement: Howard's essay of July 2023 refers to Yudkowsky's proposal of airstrikes on unauthorised data centres, which it names, as an instance of the enforcement that centralised control would require.
replies.qualification: Derivation: inferred, not explicit. The essay names Yudkowsky and his proposal of airstrikes on unauthorised data centres, not the TIME article. Premise: Yudkowsky's TIME essay of 29 March 2023 sets out that proposal. Rationale: the essay's description matches it and it was published four months earlier; the essay cites no other text. Admitted, the cites claim would be inferred, or the reply would be recorded as naming Yudkowsky with the TIME article as context. The essay's main object is the white paper "Frontier AI Regulation", which is not recorded here.

evidence.passage: Eliezer Yudkowsky, proposed airstrikes on unauthorized data centers and the threat of nuclear war to ensure compliance from states failing to control unauthorized use of computation capability

searchLog.searched: Seed texts read: Bostrom 2017 (openness); Mozilla joint statement (2023); Meta statement of support (July 2023); Zuckerberg 2024; Kapoor, Bommasani et al. 2024; Seger et al. 2023; NTIA report (July 2024); Andreessen 2023. LeCun: Senate Intelligence Committee testimony of 19 September 2023 refused (HTTP 403); his other statements on openness found were posts on X or press interviews, not used. Further texts found from seed texts' references and by web search for discovery: Goertzel and Pitt 2012 (JET); Alexander 2015; Brundage et al. 2018; Solaiman et al. 2019; EleutherAI 2021; Shevlane 2022; Narayanan and Kapoor 2023 and 2024 (AI Snake Oil); Llama 2 paper 2023; Howard 2023; Gopal et al. 2023; Hendrycks et al. 2023; Eiras et al. 2024; Bengio 2024; Ng, The Batch 257 (2024); Widder, Whittaker and West 2024. arXiv API: abs:"open source" AND abs:"model weights", and abs:"open-sourcing" AND abs:"misuse", each sorted by submission date ascending, first 50 results read by title (mostly unrelated software papers; Seger et al. was the relevant hit).
searchLog.earliestNote: Goertzel and Pitt (February 2012) is the earliest located text stating that open AGI development is probably preferable (safer) than closed; it concerns open-source AGI code, as no weights debate existed then. Bostrom 2017 and the OpenAI founding announcement of December 2015 (a dataset entity, not re-read: HTTP 403) are later. Earliest located contesting text: Alexander, 17 December 2015. No earlier text in the dataset on an overlapping concept (R15 has no dataset overlap).

searchLog.searched: Seed texts read: Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman 2013 (FHI report copy); Askell, Brundage and Hadfield 2019; Hendrycks 2023 (natural selection) and the AI-race section of Hendrycks et al. 2023; Narayanan and Kapoor 2025 (AI as Normal Technology) and their 2024 post on companies building products (read, not recorded: it concerns product-market fit, not safety). Also read: Hanson, Quillette 2023 and Overcoming Bias "AI Risk Again" (March 2023, not recorded: it concerns controlling organisations, not developer incentives); Liron, "Contra Hanson on AI Risk" (LessWrong, March 2023, read via the LessWrong API; not recorded, it does not address incentives); Bengio 2024; Hinton's Nobel banquet speech; Altman, "Machine intelligence, part 2" (2015, not recorded: it argues for regulation without addressing incentives); Andreessen 2023 (no passage on incentives producing safety). Web search for discovery: "AI companies commercial incentives safety market", Hanson 2023 posts. arXiv API: abs:"race" AND abs:"AI safety", and abs:"race to the bottom" AND cat:cs.CY, sorted ascending, first 50 read by title (later papers on racing, e.g. 2025–2026, not read in full).
searchLog.earliestNote: Among this pack's records, Hanson's Quillette essay (14 April 2023) is the earliest articulating text found. The dataset's economics collection (E04) already records Hanson's 2008 blog posts (Friendliness Factors, 16 November 2008, earliest located there) and Gans (2018, 2023); these precede it and are linked, not re-recorded. openQuestions.question: Several sources here are also read by other groups (Hendrycks et al. 2023 overview, Bengio 2024, Hinton's banquet speech, Narayanan and Kapoor 2025, Andreessen 2023). Their pack source keys and document ids may differ between drafts, and the per-source quotation budget is shared.
openQuestions.recommended: At merge, unify keys and document ids for the same expression and re-run the per-source quotation check across all drafts.

openQuestions.question: Goertzel and Pitt (2012) concern open-source AGI code and development, not model weights. Should a text predating the weights debate hold earliest-located on R15?
openQuestions.recommended: Keep it, with the qualification as written; the criterion's "open source" term covers it, and the next located texts (EleutherAI 2021) are about weights.

openQuestions.question: R17 has two articulating records against seven contesting ones, because the dataset's E04 already holds the economics texts and the other statements found were press interviews or posts on X.
openQuestions.recommended: Record the imbalance in the review note rather than admit weaker texts; consider a targeted search of law-and-economics and policy writing (liability, tort) for 2023–2026.

openQuestions.question: Andreessen (2023), NTIA (2024) and Ng (2024) are recorded as bears_on R15. A reviewer may judge Andreessen's "cat is out of the bag" and defensive-use argument to state that open release adds little marginal risk.
openQuestions.recommended: Keep as bears_on unless the reviewer finds a passage stating the marginal-risk claim directly.
